extracted.intended_audience: federal agency officials, agency policymakers, administrative-law practitioners, Congress, and ACUS members/staff
extracted.subtask_description: Formal recommendations and statements developed and adopted by the Administrative Conference of the United States to guide federal agencies, Congress, and courts on administrative procedure matters (rulemaking, adjudication, disclosure, use of algorithms, public engagement, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation development process
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations are developed by committees of ACUS members, typically with the support of expert consultants and ACUS staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed by committees of ACUS members, with expert consultants and staff support; adopted by the full membership at twice-yearly plenary sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption and publication of recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopted recommendations are published on the ACUS website and in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After adoption at plenary sessions, recommendations are published publicly (website and Federal Register) and the Chair and ACUS staff undertake activities to encourage federal agencies to carry out adopted recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-adoption follow-up and encouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chair and ACUS staff undertake activities to encourage federal agencies to carry out recommendations adopted by ACUS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACUS not only adopts recommendations but actively engages in follow-up efforts to promote agency implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements (versus recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: ACUS sometimes adopts 'Statements,' which express the agency's views on a particular matter without making a formal recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements are developed through the same process as recommendations but typically set forth issues, conclusions from a study, or comments rather than prescriptive recommendations. ACUS has adopted Statements as a distinct output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of forum for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify principles to guide Congress in choosing the appropriate forum for judicial review of agency rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rules adopted by federal agencies are generally subject to review in federal courts; ACUS has previously issued recommendations (e.g., Recommendation 75-3) to inform forum-selection principles for Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualized guidance practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies provide written guidance to explain how they propose to exercise discretionary powers and how they interpret statutes and rules; individuals request written guidance regarding how the law applies to specific circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such 'individualized guidance' goes by various names and agency practices vary; recommendations address how agencies should provide and manage individualized guidance requests and explanations about application of law to particular requesters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of senate-confirmed officials in adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of the participation of Senate-confirmed (PAS) officials in administrative adjudication alongside career civil servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many federal officials—including PAS officials—participate in adjudication; recommendations examine how PAS officials work with career staff to structure adjudicative processes and the implications for procedure and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of congressional constituent service inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should recognize and manage the role of congressional constituent service inquiries submitted on behalf of constituents seeking help accessing federal programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thousands contact their representatives who then submit requests to agencies; recommendations address agency processes for handling constituent inquiries given their role in agency-congressional relations and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of algorithmic tools in regulatory enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies considering AI and other algorithmic tools for enforcement must weigh potential benefits (lowering cost, improving quality, consistency, predictability) against concerns these tools raise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmic tools hold promises for efficiency and decision quality but also raise concerns (implicit in the recommendation); agencies should assess both potential benefits and risks when deploying such tools in enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public engagement under the good cause exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when invoking the 'good cause' exemption from notice-and-comment, agencies should facilitate public participation through engagement activities designed to elicit input, enhance understanding of the rulemaking process, and foster meaningful participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public participation plays an essential role in rulemaking; ACUS recommends agencies use engagement activities to elicit input and broaden meaningful participation, even in contexts where the formal notice-and-comment process is bypassed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonlawyer assistance and representation in adjudications
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies can increase access to representation and assistance in administrative adjudications by permitting qualified nonlawyers to practice before them and supporting other forms of assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many participants cannot access lawyers, agencies should consider permitting qualified nonlawyer advocates and other support mechanisms to improve access to representation in adjudicative proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive disclosure of agency legal materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies produce many legal materials that establish, interpret, apply, explain, or address enforcement of legal rights and obligations; proactive disclosure is needed to address inconsistencies in disclosure practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal statutes govern disclosure but inconsistencies exist across agencies and materials; ACUS recommends proactive publication practices to improve public access and clarity regarding agency legal materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual public engagement for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should use virtual, Internet-based videoconferencing and other online engagement tools to broaden participation in rulemakings and reduce barriers to participation, particularly for historically underserved communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtual engagement, increasingly used (especially during the COVID-19 pandemic), can help expand access and inclusivity in public participation for rulemaking processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic tools for retrospective review
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may leverage algorithmic/AI tools in retrospective review to efficiently identify rules that are outmoded, redundant, contain typographic errors, or have inaccurate cross-references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retrospective review can be made more efficient and accurate using algorithmic methods to flag candidate rules for update or repeal and to detect technical errors needing correction.
